The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of African moonfish (Selene dorsalis) has been measured at 5.6% [GSI = 5.6%] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C]. Such a strategy is not uncommon among members of the genus Selene, which are known for their laterally compressed bodies and habitual occupation of shallow, productive coastal waters.

This species exhibits a total length at puberty for females of 21.29 centimeters [Lp = 21.29 centimeters], a size that marks the onset of functional ovarian activity and the capacity to participate in spawning aggregations. Reaching this milestone corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 253.7 grams [Wwp = 253.7 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic growth required before energetic resources are redirected toward gamete production. The relationship between these two metrics implies a relatively late onset of maturity for a fish of this moderate body plan, a trait that may render local populations particularly sensitive to size-selective fishing pressure. Understanding these thresholds is essential for the implementation of slot-limit regulations designed to protect the reproductive portion of the stock.

Neonatal individuals emerge from the egg chorion after an incubation period lasting a mere 1.4 days [ab = 1.4 days] when water temperatures are held at 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C], a developmental pace that places this species among the faster-hatching carangids. The wet weight at birth of these yolk-sac larvae is exceptionally small, estimated at a mass of 0.000278 grams [Wwb = 0.000278 grams], a value derived from the species' egg diameter and reflecting the limited endogenous reserves available to the newly hatched alevin. This minimal initial mass necessitates an extremely rapid transition to exogenous feeding, typically occurring within hours of eclosion, to prevent starvation. The first feeding stage is therefore a critical bottleneck in the early life history, with larval survival heavily contingent upon the synchronized availability of suitable microzooplankton prey in the pelagic environment.

The ultimate total length attained by adult African moonfish has been documented at 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], representing the maximum recorded size for the species and corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 1143 grams [Wwi = 1143 grams]. This allometric relationship, derived from length-weight regressions applied to large-bodied individuals, indicates that the species achieves a robust, deep-bodied form characteristic of the genus. Such an upper size limit places Selene dorsalis among the medium-sized carangids inhabiting the eastern Atlantic shelf, where it occupies a trophic niche as a visual predator of small fishes and crustaceans. The maximum documented lifespan for this species, recorded under stable thermal conditions at 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C], is approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years], indicating a relatively slow pace of life given its moderate body size and a reproductive lifespan that includes many spawning seasons.

Under the same stable thermal regime of 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C], the longevity record of about ten thousand nine hundred and fifty days [am = about ten thousand nine hundred and fifty days] underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over a single, explosive reproductive episode. The contrast between the rapid embryonic development, which takes only 1.4 days [ab = 1.4 days], and the long adult lifespan highlights a striking ontogenetic shift in mortality risk: fast, vulnerable early stages give way to a long-lived, low-mortality adult phase at a temperature of 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C]. Such a pattern is typical of marine fishes that have evolved in environments where juvenile predation is intense but adult predation is comparatively relaxed.
